title: Ask, don't tell
hookLine: don't dwell on your own deeds and dangers; others don't enjoy them as you do (Enchiridion 33)
carry: hands the stage to someone else
last: A WORD THAT DOESN'T NEED HELP.

lines: THE THIRD TIME YOU'VE HEARD IT.
cards: Everyone has been on the receiving end of this. Dinner, a long table, and someone is telling the story of their near miss on the highway. Or the marathon.
Or the time they told the boss exactly what they thought. It's the third time you've heard it, and it's getting longer. The uncomfortable part: everyone has also been the one telling it.
Section thirty-three, still sketching how to behave in company, has a line for exactly this.

teach.h: DON'T DWELL ON YOUR OWN EXPLOITS.
teach.b: In company, Epictetus says, don't keep bringing up your own deeds and your own dangers, often and at length.

teach.h: YOUR DANGERS THRILL YOU, NOT THEM.
teach.b: The reason is disarmingly honest: however pleasant it is for you to recall your dangers, it isn't as pleasant for other people to hear about them. No grand theory.
Just an observation anyone can check at the next dinner party. Your own stories glow for you because you were in them. For everyone else, they're secondhand.
Avoid playing for laughs, he says. It slides easily into vulgarity, and it tends to lower the respect the people around you have for you. The common thread is the spotlight.

Telling your adventures and working the room for a laugh both turn a conversation into a stage with one performer. Now the turn. The handbook doesn't say ask in so many words; that's how this path carries it.
But it fits the man Epictetus admired most.
Socrates, in Plato's dialogues, is well-known for asking questions, so many that it became a method named after him. If you're not telling, you have room to ask. How was your week?
What happened next? What was that like for you? A question hands the stage to someone else.
It's a small trade: one story fewer told, one more heard all the way to the end.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes set themselves a simple conversational habit: fewer stories about their own exploits and more questions about the other person.

o: to hand the talk over with a question, not a story
to tell your best story so the table stays lively
to request a favor politely from someone you know

games.q: ask, don't tell — tap the pairs.
p: pleasant for you, less for them

s: Epictetus says other people enjoy your adventure stories as much as you do
his whole point is that they don't.
the word ask appears in the handbook's rule
the rule is about not telling; ask is how this path carries it.
right after this rule, he warns against playing for laughs
it slides into vulgarity and lowers people's respect.

games.q: a friend mentions a scary drive home last night. you had a scarier one last year. what fits Epictetus' advice?
o: tell yours. it's a better story.
change the subject to something funnier.
games.why: he says not to dwell on your own dangers; others don't enjoy them as you do. asking keeps the stage where it belongs.

practice: Think of someone you'll talk with today, a coworker, a friend, a parent, a child, the person at the counter, and picture the moment you'd usually start telling them your news.
Picture asking them a question instead, and actually waiting for the answer. Keep one ready: how are you, really, or what's been the best part of your week?

wordCard.voice: Ask. Enchiridion thirty-three: don't keep telling your own deeds and dangers. Others don't enjoy them as much as you do. Leave room to ask. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: danger. Enchiridion 33 warns against dwelling on your own.

carryVoice: Your line: hands the stage to someone else. That's what a good question does. That's day three hundred sixty-seven.
